Unmet driving hours occur when battery charging is not sufficient for the EV’s energy demand and are primarily a result of modeling limitations. The most important factors determining unmet driving hours are charger level, VMT, and percent charged at home. Charger level influences the rate of charging possible, while VMT and percent charged at home determine the amount of charging needed. Figure 6 highlights this trend, where only vehicles with high VMT and a high rate of home charging incur unmet driving hours. The decrease in this measure is due to the larger fraction of homes with L2 chargers, which are more likely to meet the vehicle’s energy demand compared to L1 chargers. Vehicles with high VMT are relatively uncommon, and most vehicles in the stock experience no unmet driving hours. Across the entire stock, this measure results in an average of 0.35 unmet driving hours, affecting 2.17% of homes. Figure 6. Unmet driving hours occur when battery charging is not sufficient for the EV's energy demand. 5.3 Peak Considerations Figure 7 shows the electricity demand for the state of Colorado over 3 days in the winter (left) and 3 days in the summer (right). The dashed line is the demand from the baseline scenario. This measure results in new electricity peaks coinciding with the average time an occupant returns home and aligns closely with the timing of the baseline daily peaks in both seasons. Note that this measure is not meant to reflect a realistic scenario on its own. Rather, it is designed to offer the users flexibility when combined with the baseline or other measures. As such, results should be interpreted with caution and not assumed to reflect real-world outcomes. 15 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications.
